newsitem.title: USA: Republicans propose aid for welfare immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Republicans propose aid for welfare immigrants.

text.p: House Republicans Wednesday tentatively agreed to provide states $125 million in short-term aid to care for legal immigrants who will lose federal benefits under a controversial new welfare law.
The funding could be debated by a House committee as early as Thursday. Under the welfare law hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants are slated to lose Food Stamps and disability aid by August 22.

The new funding would be aimed at elderly frail immigrants who are not likely to qualify for citizenship due to lack of language skills or or other problems. It would be the first installment of what some Republican lawmakers hope will be a larger aid package.

Florida Republican Rep. Clay Shaw said the money was intended to aid states only through September 30, the end of the budget year. But he admitted lawmakers were having a hard time finding offsetting spending cuts in other federal programs that would be needed to fund a bigger aid package.
"I would be happy to continue some assistance to aliens that are truly disabled and don't have any other means of support. The problem is to find that kind of money. That's a tough one," Shaw said.
Shaw had originally talked about a two-year, $2 billion program.
The proposal was debated during an afternoon meeting with top lawmakers and House Speaker Newt Gingrich. The Senate has been considering a similiar funding level.

It could be attached to an emergency spending bill now moving through the House Appropriations Committee providing $5.3 billion for disaster relief in more than 20 states and $2 billion for peacekeeping forces in Bosnia.

More than 40 percent of total savings in the welfare law come from denying benefits to legal aliens. As the deadline for ending aid to legal immigrants approaches, pressure is building for Congress to act.

President Clinton's balanced budget plan would restore about $15 billion to immigrants. It would guarantee aid to immigrants disabled after entering the United States but continues Food Stamps only through Sept. 30, 1997.
Republicans have insisted they will not reopen the welfare law, but want to provide some aid to frail, elderly immigrants who cannot qualify for citizenship for a host of reasons.
Advocates for the poor have sued to block the law in New York and California.

Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles is also taking the federal government to court over the issue. Chiles said Florida will have to pay more than $1 billion a year to care for immigrants who will lose federal aid.
